Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
k=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor ,
\]

so that \(k^2\le n<(k+1)^2\). We analyze prime powers dividing \(n\).

Let \(p^a\Vert n\), meaning \(p^a\mid n\) but \(p^{a+1}\nmid n\).

---

### 1. Prime factors \(p\le k\)

If \(p\le k\), then \(p\mid k!\), so

\[
v_p\bigl((k!)^{n!}\bigr)=n!\,v_p(k!)\ge n!.
\]

Also \(p^a\le n\), so \(a\le \log_2 n\le n\le n!\) for \(n\ge4\). Since \(p\le k\) forces \(n\ge p^2\ge4\), we get

\[
v_p\bigl((k!)^{n!}\bigr)\ge a.
\]

Thus \(p^a\mid (k!)^{n!}\). Since \(n\mid (k!)^{n!}+450\), it follows that

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

Therefore every prime factor of \(n\) that is \(\le k\) must be among

\[
2,3,5,
\]

and its exponent is bounded by its exponent in \(450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2\).

---

### 2. Prime factors \(p>k\)

If \(p>k\), then \(p\nmid k!\). Also, since \(p\mid n\), we have \(p\le n\), so \(p-1\le n\) and hence

\[
p-1\mid n!.
\]

By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(k!)^{n!}\equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]

Thus the divisibility condition gives

\[
1+450\equiv 0\pmod p,
\]

so

\[
p\mid 451.
\]

Since

\[
451=11\cdot 41,
\]

any prime factor of \(n\) greater than \(k\) must be \(11\) or \(41\).

Also, if \(p>k\), then \(p\ge k+1\), so

\[
p^2\ge (k+1)^2>n,
\]

meaning such a prime can appear only to the first power. Moreover, there can be at most one prime factor of \(n\) greater than \(k\), since two distinct primes \(p,q>k\) would give

\[
n\ge pq\ge (k+1)^2,
\]

contradicting \(n<(k+1)^2\).

---

### 3. Bounding \(n\)

So \(n\) has one of the following forms.

#### Case 1: No prime factor exceeds \(k\)

Then every prime power in \(n\) divides \(450\), so

\[
n\mid 450.
\]

Thus \(n\le 450\).

#### Case 2: One prime factor exceeds \(k\)

Then

\[
n=dp,
\]

where \(p\in\{11,41\}\), \(p>k\), and \(d\mid 450\).

Since \(p>k\), we have \(p^2>n=pd\), so

\[
d<p.
\]

- If \(p=11\), then \(d<11\). Since \(d\mid 450\), the largest possible \(d\) is \(10\), giving \(n\le 110\).

- If \(p=41\), then \(d<41\). The largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(41\) is \(30\). Hence

\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

Therefore any valid \(n\) satisfies

\[
n\le 1230.
\]

---

### 4. Check that \(n=1230\) works

For \(n=1230\),

\[
\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\rfloor =35,
\]

and

\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

We check divisibility by each prime factor.

- Modulo \(2,3,5\): Since \(35!\) is divisible by each of \(2,3,5\), and \(450\) is also divisible by each of \(2,3,5\),

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 0\pmod{2,3,5}.
\]

- Modulo \(41\): Since \(41>35\), \(35!\not\equiv 0\pmod{41}\). Also \(40\mid 1230!\), so by Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Thus

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod{41},
\]

because \(451=11\cdot 41\).

Since \(1230\) is squarefree and each prime divisor of \(1230\) divides the expression, we have

\[
1230\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

Hence the largest possible \(n\) is

\[
\boxed{1230}.
\]
